frase_gancho.texto: A pair of monuments, round altar and stela, better known in the south of Mesoamerica.

puente_narrativo.texto: Follow your route: what comes next is sculpted into the hill itself.

guion_corto.texto: At Chalcatzingo there are pairs of stones you would not expect to find in central Mexico: a round altar beside a stela. In a stone-faced mound with platforms, a mutilated stela that was still standing was found in nineteen seventy-four, Monument Twenty-seven. To the north, a large circular altar, Monument Twenty-five, beside the base of another large stela, Monument Twenty-six. At the other end lies the base of a third stela, Monument Thirty-four, beside a round altar, Monument Forty. This combination is characteristic of the south of Mesoamerica. Here it appears in its oldest examples from Central Mexico.

guion_largo.texto:
A stela and a round altar. Two stones, one standing and one low. That pair is the protagonist of this stop, and it says a lot about how Chalcatzingo related to distant regions.

In nineteen seventy-four, the Chalcatzingo Archaeological Project excavated a mound with platforms faced with stones. There a mutilated Middle Preclassic stela appeared, still standing: Monument Twenty-seven.

To the north of the platform, a large circular altar was discovered, Monument Twenty-five, beside the lower part of a large stela, Monument Twenty-six.

At the opposite end, Grove's excavations in nineteen ninety-eight uncovered the broken base of a second stela, Monument Thirty-four. The recent work of INAH, in the same area, found a round altar, Monument Forty, beside that base.

Why the discovery of two stela bases associated with round altars matters. According to Grove, that combination is not common in the Central Highlands. It is characteristic of the south of Mesoamerica: of Chiapas, of the Pacific coast of Guatemala, and of the Maya Lowlands. It does not exist at the Olmec sites of the Gulf Coast. The two cases at Chalcatzingo are the earliest examples recorded in Central Mexico.

There is more. On all four sides of the base of the stela of Monument Thirty-four, traces of carved designs remain. They include fragments of motifs with scrolls and with mats. Grove explains that those motifs are, stylistically, typical of the sculptures of Chiapas and of the Maya region of the Late Preclassic.

A round altar is a low stone, circular in shape, set beside a stela. A stela is a tall stone that stands upright. Together they form a pair that archaeologists recognize in places very far from here.

The Late Preclassic is the stage that follows the Middle Preclassic. That a motif from Chiapas or from the Maya of that stage appears at Chalcatzingo does not prove that the builders traveled all the way there. But it does show that certain forms circulated between regions.

What ceremonies were held before these pairs is something the sources consulted do not specify. What we do know is where they stood and what makes them rare in Central Mexico.

The pairs appeared at different times. The mutilated stela, Monument Twenty-seven, was excavated in nineteen seventy-four. The base of Monument Thirty-four was discovered by Grove in nineteen ninety-eight. The round altar of Monument Forty was uncovered by the most recent work of INAH.

If you put it together with what you saw in the sunken patio, the picture is completed. A wall with a motif that appears in Guerrero and in Morelos. An altar-throne that recalls the Gulf Coast. A pair of altar and stela that points south. Chalcatzingo did not copy a single model. It took ideas from several places and combined them.

Now the landscape changes. The hill comes next, and with it the reliefs carved into the rock.

texto.pregunta: Myth: Altars and stelae are an Olmec invention.
texto.respuesta: Reality: The pair of round altar and stela does not exist at the Olmec sites of the Gulf; it is characteristic of the south of Mesoamerica.
